notes.meaning: The men of Kiriath-jearim faithfully came and brought the ark of the LORD to their town, placing it in the home of Abinadab on the hill. His son Eleazar was set apart to guard the holy chest and treat it with proper care. Shiloh was no longer available as a home for the ark, likely having been destroyed after the earlier defeat by the Philistines.

A full twenty years passed while the ark stayed in Kiriath-jearim, until the whole nation of Israel began to grieve over their sins and long for the LORD. Having the ark back in the land had not automatically fixed their hearts, but Samuel worked quietly among them during this long wait. At last, the people were ready to seek God in earnest.

Samuel challenged the people to prove that their sorrow was real by getting rid of their idols, including the false Canaanite gods and the goddess Ashtoreth. He told them to set their hearts completely on the LORD and worship Him alone. True deliverance from Philistine oppression would come only when their devotion to God was sincere.

The Israelites listened to Samuel and tore down their images of Baal and Ashtoreth, choosing to serve the LORD alone. Removing these false gods was a bold step that proved their repentance was genuine. It also showed courage, because throwing away the idols was an open act of defiance against the Philistines who ruled them.

Samuel directed the people to gather as one body at Mizpah, a high and well-known meeting place. He did not call them together to organize an army, but to stand before God as their praying mediator. His offer to intercede showed that Israel's true hope lay in prayer rather than military strength.

At Mizpah, the people poured out water on the ground and fasted, showing their deep sorrow and helplessness before God. They openly confessed their sins, holding nothing back. In that sacred assembly, Samuel also stepped forward to govern and guide the nation as their judge.

Hearing about the large gathering at Mizpah, the Philistine rulers marched up with their troops to crush what looked like a rebellion. The Israelites were terrified because they were assembled for worship and not equipped for a battle against seasoned warriors. Their fear, however, drove them to seek God instead of running away.

The people begged Samuel not to stop crying out to the LORD for them so that God would rescue them from the Philistines. Unlike their earlier mistake of treating the ark like a good-luck charm, they now placed their trust in God Himself through the prayers of His servant. They knew that human effort alone could never save them.

Samuel took a young nursing lamb and offered it completely on the altar as a burnt offering to the LORD, showing total dedication and a plea for pardon. At the same time, he cried out to God on Israel's behalf. God heard his cry and answered him with favor.

Just as the Philistine army closed in to attack while the sacrifice was still being offered, the LORD spoke from heaven with a mighty crash of thunder. The sudden tempest threw the Philistines into wild panic and confusion, causing their ranks to break and flee. God fought directly for His people just as Hannah had once prophesied.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that Baal was worshipped as the master of the storm, so the LORD using thunder to defeat the enemy was a direct show of power over the Canaanite idol.

notes.meaning: Encouraged by God's intervention, the men of Israel rushed out from Mizpah and chased the fleeing Philistines down the rocky hills. They struck down the enemy forces all the way to an area below Beth-car. An army that began the day in trembling fear ended it in complete victory.

After the battle, Samuel set up a large stone between Mizpah and Shen as an enduring monument of the victory. He named it Ebenezer, which means 'stone of help,' declaring that the LORD had helped them every step of the way up to that moment. This dramatic triumph took place near the very site where Israel had suffered a tragic defeat twenty years before.

The Philistines were thoroughly humbled and stopped launching major invasions into Israelite territory during Samuel's leadership. The LORD's mighty hand remained against them throughout his days, keeping them in check. God gave His people a prolonged season of relief from the heavy oppression they had suffered.

Israel recovered the border towns and surrounding lands that the Philistines had previously taken, stretching along the frontier from Ekron to Gath. The neighboring Amorites also made peace with Israel, realizing that the Israelites had regained strength under God's protection. The victory brought security across the entire region.

Samuel continued to serve as Israel's judge for the rest of his life. Even after Saul was later anointed as king to lead the army, Samuel kept his special role as God's prophet and spiritual guide for the nation. He was faithful in serving God and helping his people until his final days.

Each year Samuel traveled on a regular circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah to hold court and settle disputes among the people. By traveling to these key centers, he made justice easy to reach and kept close watch over the spiritual health of the community. His faithful rounds helped unite the tribes under God's law.

After completing his travels, Samuel would return home to Ramah, where he lived and also judged the people. There he built an altar to the LORD so he could offer sacrifices and pray for the nation. Because the tabernacle at Shiloh was gone, God accepted worship at this altar as Samuel sought His guidance.
